lessons.title: Diagnosing Common Building Defects
lessons.body: Before you repair anything, you must know what is wrong and why. Start by walking around the building with a notebook, a torch, a small mirror, and a camera or phone. Look for cracks, damp patches, crumbling mortar, rotten timber, and loose roof sheets. In Africa, common defects include rising damp from poor drainage, termite damage in timber, and cracks from ground movement during dry and wet seasons. Check walls for vertical cracks wider than 3mm â these are structural and need an engineer. Hairline cracks (under 1mm) are usually plaster shrinkage and can be filled. Use a 2m straight edge or a string line to check if walls are bulging or leaning. Tap walls with a hammer: a hollow sound means plaster has separated from the wall. For damp, look for dark patches at the base of walls, musty smells, and peeling paint. A simple moisture meter (costing about $30) or a piece of plastic taped to the wall for 24 hours can show condensation versus rising damp. Check roofs from inside: water stains on ceiling boards mean leaks. Outside, look for broken tiles, rusted sheets, and blocked gutters. For timber, probe with a screwdriver â if it sinks in easily, the wood is rotten. Termites leave mud tubes on foundations and walls. Always diagnose the cause, not just the symptom. For example, a crack might be from a leaking gutter eroding the foundation. Write down the location, size, and likely cause of each defect. Take photos with a ruler for scale. This record becomes your repair plan and helps you track if defects get worse. Never start repairs without a diagnosis, or you will waste money and the problem will return.

lessons.title: Masonry Repair: Mortars and Pointing
lessons.body: Masonry repairs in Africa often fail because people use cement-rich mortars that are too hard. Old buildings were built with lime mortars that are soft and breathable. If you patch them with strong cement, the patch will crack and damage the original bricks. First, remove loose mortar with a plugging chisel and a soft brush. Never use a grinder â it damages brick edges. For lime mortar, mix 1 part lime putty (or hydrated lime) to 3 parts sharp sand by volume. Add water slowly until it's like peanut butter. For cement-lime mortar, use 1 part cement, 1 part lime, and 6 parts sand. Let it sit for 10 minutes, then mix again. Before pointing, wet the joints with a spray bottle so the mortar doesn't dry too fast. Push mortar into joints with a pointing trowel or a wooden stick, filling to the depth of the joint. Don't smear it on the brick face. Let it set for 30 minutes, then finish with a wooden stick or a stiff brush to match the original profile. Cure the mortar by spraying with water twice a day for 3 days. In hot, dry climates, cover with damp cloth. For cracks wider than 5mm, use a lime grout: mix lime, sand, and water to a creamy consistency and pour into the crack in layers. For deep holes, pack in lime mortar in 10mm layers, letting each layer set before adding the next. If you see white salt deposits (efflorescence), brush it off dry and find the water source â usually a leak. Never paint over damp masonry; it traps moisture. Always wear gloves and a dust mask when mixing. Test your mortar on a small area first. Good pointing lasts 50 years or more.

lessons.title: Timber Repair: Splicing and Consolidation
lessons.body: Timber in African buildings often suffers from termites, rot, and sun damage. Before repairing, identify the extent. Probe with an awl or screwdriver. If the wood is soft and crumbly, it's rotten. If you see mud tubes, termites are active. First, treat the area with a borate-based preservative (mix 1 part borax to 1 part boric acid in 10 parts water). Brush it on all exposed wood. For minor rot, remove the soft wood with a chisel until you reach solid timber. Treat the cavity with preservative, then fill with a two-part epoxy wood filler (available at hardware stores). For structural timbers like beams or rafters, you need splicing. Cut out the rotten section with a saw, making a clean square cut. Cut a new piece of treated timber of the same size, but make a scarf joint (a diagonal cut) so the two pieces overlap by at least 4 times the timber's thickness. For example, a 100mm x 100mm beam needs a 400mm overlap. Drill holes and use galvanized bolts or screws every 100mm in a zigzag pattern. Apply waterproof wood glue between the surfaces before bolting. For consolidation of historic timber, you can inject epoxy resin into cracks. Drill 10mm holes at 45 degrees along the crack, insert plastic ports, seal with putty, and inject low-viscosity epoxy until it comes out the next port. This is advanced work â practice on scrap wood first. Always support the structure with props before cutting. After repair, paint or varnish the timber to protect it. In termite-prone areas, keep wood at least 150mm above soil and use treated timber. Check repairs every 6 months.

lessons.title: Roof and Gutter Maintenance
lessons.body: Roofs and gutters fail faster than any other part of a building. In Africa, common problems are rusted corrugated iron sheets, cracked tiles, and blocked gutters that cause damp walls. Start with a roof inspection twice a year â before the rainy season and after. Use a ladder with a helper. Never walk on a fragile roof without crawling boards. Look for loose nails, lifted sheets, and rust. For small holes in iron sheets, clean the area with a wire brush, then apply a bitumen-based roof patch or a self-adhesive flashing tape. For larger holes, cut a piece of galvanized sheet slightly larger than the hole, apply roof sealant, and screw it down with rubber washers. Replace rusted sheets if more than 30% of the surface is rusted. For tiles, replace broken ones by lifting the tiles above, sliding out the broken tile, and sliding in a new one. Secure with a copper wire or a clip. Gutters: clean them at least twice a year, more if you have trees. Use a scoop or your hands with gloves. Flush with a hose. Check the slope: gutters should fall 1cm for every 3 metres toward the downpipe. If water pools, adjust the brackets. Fix leaks in gutters with silicone sealant or a patch of the same material. For thatched roofs, check for loose thatch and replace with new bundles, overlapping by 50%. In coastal areas, use stainless steel or plastic gutters to resist salt. Always wear non-slip shoes and harness if working at height. Keep a record of repairs so you know when to replace. A well-maintained roof lasts 20-30 years.

lessons.title: Window and Door Repair Techniques
lessons.body: Windows and doors stick, rot, and break â but most repairs are simple. First, check if the frame is square. Open the window or door and look at the gaps. If it sticks at the top, the hinges may be loose or the frame has swollen. Tighten hinge screws; if they won't hold, fill the holes with wooden matchsticks and glue, then re-screw. For swollen timber, plane the edge lightly with a block plane. Sand with 80-grit then 120-grit paper. For metal windows, check for rust. Remove rust with a wire brush and apply red oxide primer, then paint. If a window won't latch, adjust the strike plate or file the latch. For broken glass, remove all shards, wear gloves. Measure the opening, subtract 3mm for clearance. Apply glazing putty around the rebate, press in the glass, then add more putty and smooth with a putty knife. Let it skin for 7 days before painting. For wooden doors that drag, remove the door by unscrewing hinges. Plane the bottom or side that rubs. Seal all edges with paint or varnish to prevent moisture. For locks that jam, spray with graphite powder, not oil (oil attracts dust). If a door is warped, you may need to replace it. For security, add a second lock or a metal plate. In humid areas, use stainless steel hinges and screws. Check windows and doors every 3 months. Lubricate hinges with a few drops of machine oil. Replace broken handles immediately. A well-maintained door lasts 50 years.

lessons.title: Creating a Cyclical Maintenance Program
lessons.body: A cyclical maintenance program means you plan repairs before they become emergencies. Start by making a building inventory: list every component â roof, walls, gutters, windows, doors, plumbing, electrical. For each, note its condition (good, fair, poor) and the last time it was repaired. Then set a schedule. For example: clean gutters every 6 months; check roof twice a year; repaint timber every 5 years; service plumbing annually. Use a simple spreadsheet or a notebook with columns for date, task, who did it, and cost. In Africa, align tasks with seasons: before the rains, check roof and drainage; after the rains, check for damp and cracks. Budget 1-2% of the building's value per year for maintenance. For a $50,000 building, that's $500-$1,000 per year. Break it into monthly savings. Train a caretaker or assign one person to do monthly walk-arounds. They should look for leaks, cracks, pests, and blocked drains. Keep a log of every repair, with photos. Use a simple colour code: green (no action), yellow (monitor), red (repair now). For communal buildings, involve users â teach them to report problems. Set up a maintenance committee that meets quarterly. Use local materials and skills to keep costs low. For example, make your own lime mortar or borrow scaffolding from a neighbour. Always keep spare parts: roof screws, washers, glazing putty, fuses. After each repair, update the schedule. Review the whole program once a year and adjust. A good program prevents small defects from becoming big bills. It also preserves the building for future generations. Start today with a simple checklist.

quiz.q: What is the first step in diagnosing building defects?
options: B) Walk around with a notebook and tools
quiz.explanation: Diagnosis requires systematic observation using basic tools before any repair.

quiz.q: Which crack width usually indicates a structural problem?
quiz.explanation: Cracks wider than 3mm often need an engineer because they may affect stability.

quiz.q: What does a hollow sound when tapping a wall mean?
quiz.explanation: A hollow sound indicates delamination of plaster from the substrate.

quiz.q: How can you distinguish rising damp from condensation?
options: A) Rising damp is always high up
C) Tape plastic on wall for 24 hours
quiz.explanation: The plastic test shows moisture trapped underneath for rising damp, while condensation appears on the surface.

quiz.q: What is a sign of termite activity in timber?
quiz.explanation: Termites build mud tubes on foundations and walls to travel.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid cement-rich mortar on old buildings?
options: B) It's too hard and damages bricks
quiz.explanation: Cement-rich mortar is harder than historic bricks and causes cracking and damage.

quiz.q: What is the correct ratio for lime mortar?
quiz.explanation: A 1:3 lime to sand mix by volume is standard for repointing historic masonry.

quiz.q: How should you finish mortar joints?
options: B) Use a wooden stick or stiff brush
quiz.explanation: Finishing with a wooden stick or brush matches the original profile without smearing.

quiz.q: How long should you cure lime mortar?
quiz.explanation: Spray with water twice a day for 3 days to cure properly.

quiz.q: What should you do before pointing old masonry?
quiz.explanation: Wetting the joints prevents the mortar from drying too quickly and cracking.

quiz.q: What is the first step in timber repair?
quiz.explanation: Probing identifies the extent of rot or termite damage.

quiz.q: What is a scarf joint?
quiz.explanation: A scarf joint is a diagonal cut that overlaps two pieces of timber for splicing.

quiz.q: How long should the overlap be for a scarf joint?
quiz.explanation: The overlap should be at least 4 times the timber's thickness for strength.

quiz.q: What is consolidation in timber repair?
quiz.explanation: Consolidation involves injecting resin to fill cracks and strengthen timber.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect a roof?
quiz.explanation: Twice a year, before and after the rainy season, is recommended.

quiz.q: What is the correct slope for gutters?
quiz.explanation: A fall of 1cm for every 3 metres ensures water flows to the downpipe.

quiz.q: How should you repair a small hole in a corrugated iron sheet?
options: B) Use bitumen patch or flashing tape
quiz.explanation: Bitumen patch or self-adhesive flashing tape is a simple, effective repair.

quiz.q: What should you do if a window sticks?
options: B) Check hinges and plane if swollen
quiz.explanation: Tighten hinges and plane swollen timber to fix sticking.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to replace broken glass?
options: B) Apply glazing putty, press glass, add more putty
quiz.explanation: Glazing putty seals the glass and allows for movement.

quiz.q: What should you use to lubricate a jammed lock?
quiz.explanation: Graphite powder lubricates without attracting dust like oil does.

quiz.q: What is the first step in creating a maintenance program?
quiz.explanation: An inventory lists all components and their condition.

quiz.q: How much of a building's value should be budgeted for annual maintenance?
quiz.explanation: 1-2% of building value per year is a standard maintenance budget.

quiz.q: When should you clean gutters in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning every 6 months, before and after rains, prevents blockages.

quiz.q: What does a red code in a maintenance log mean?
quiz.explanation: Red indicates an urgent repair needed immediately.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep spare parts?
quiz.explanation: Spare parts allow immediate repairs, preventing further damage.

quiz.q: What is a cyclical maintenance program?
quiz.explanation: It is a planned schedule of inspections and repairs to prevent emergencies.

quiz.q: How can you test for rising damp?
quiz.explanation: Taping plastic shows moisture trapped underneath if rising damp is present.

quiz.q: What is the correct mix for cement-lime mortar?
quiz.explanation: A 1:1:6 mix provides a moderate strength mortar suitable for many repairs.

quiz.q: What should you do before cutting a structural timber?
quiz.explanation: Props prevent collapse during cutting and splicing.

quiz.q: How often should you review your maintenance program?
quiz.explanation: An annual review allows adjustments based on performance and new issues.
